title: Back then, as a child
goal: Add the second past tense — the one that describes **habits and background** in the past, not single events. English often blurs the two with "used to" and "was …-ing"; Portuguese gives it its own verb form.
bekal: choosing between the two past tenses according to the kind of story
describing your childhood and old habits

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Fotos antigas
dialogs.intro: Carla is showing an old album at her grandmother's house. Budi looks on.

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: Olha, essa era a nossa casa antiga.
lines.id: Look, this was our old house.
lines.literal: look, this it-was the our house old.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: How pretty! Did you live there?

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: Morei até os dez anos. Era pequena, mas tinha um quintal enorme.
lines.id: Until I was ten. It was small, but it had a huge backyard.
lines.literal: I-lived until the(pl) ten years. it-was small, but it-had a backyard enormous.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: What did you use to do there?

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: Eu brincava com os vizinhos todo dia depois da escola.
lines.id: I played with the neighbors every day after school.
lines.literal: I I-played with the(pl) neighbors every day after of-the school.

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: De pique-esconde, de bola... A gente ficava na rua até escurecer.
lines.id: Hide-and-seek, ball games... We'd stay out in the street until dark.
lines.literal: of tag-hide, of ball... the people stayed in-the street until get-dark.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Aqui era assim também. E a sua avó, cozinhava muito?
lines.id: It was like that for me too. And your grandma, did she cook a lot?
lines.literal: here it-was like-that also. and the your grandmother, she-cooked much?

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: Todo domingo. A casa inteira cheirava a feijoada.
lines.id: Every Sunday. The whole house smelled of feijoada.
lines.literal: every Sunday. the house whole it-smelled to feijoada.

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: Sinto, sim. Mas um dia a gente vendeu a casa e mudou pra cá.
lines.id: I do. But one day we sold the house and moved here.
lines.literal: I-feel, yes. but one day the people sold the house and moved to here.

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: Naquela época eu chorei muito. Hoje eu entendo.
lines.id: Back then I cried a lot. Now I understand.
lines.literal: in-that time I I-cried much. today I I-understand.

notes: **Two past tenses sit side by side in this dialogue, and the difference isn't about time but about the shape of the story.** *Morava* describes a long-lasting state with no clear start or end; *morei até os dez anos* names one span that's now closed. *Brincava* describes a habit; *vendeu* and *chorei* name events that happened once.

**Saudade** is the world's most famous Portuguese word, and it's often called untranslatable. It means longing for something far away or gone — a person, a place, a time. *Que saudade!* = "I miss it so much!", *Estou com saudade de você* = "I miss you". English "miss" covers part of it, but *saudade* carries a sweet ache that "miss" doesn't quite capture.

**Brincar de** — to play at something. Note the *de*: *brincar de bola*, *brincar de pique-esconde*. ⚠️ *Brincar* also means "to joke": *Tô brincando!* = "Just kidding!" For real sports, the verb is *jogar*: *jogar futebol*.
**Naquela época** = *em + aquela época*, "at that time". A pointing word fused with a preposition, as you saw in unit 13. It's one of the most common openers for a story about the past.
**Mudar pra cá** = "to move here". *Cá* is a casual form of *aqui*, and appears almost only in phrases like *vem cá* ("come here") and *pra cá*.

grammars.title: Imperfeito — the describing past
body: Its endings are much simpler than the first past tense, and the -er and -ir groups use **exactly the same** endings.
after: **The *eu* and *ele* forms are identical.** If you need to be clear, say the pronoun: *eu falava* versus *ele falava*. In practice, context is almost always enough.

**Only four verbs are irregular in this tense** — a tiny number compared with the first past tense: *ser* → **era, éramos, eram**; *ter* → **tinha, tínhamos, tinham**; *vir* → **vinha, vínhamos, vinham**; *pôr* → **punha, púnhamos, punham**. Everything else is regular, no exceptions.
⚠️ *Era* and *tinha* are the two forms you'll use most from this whole unit. *Era pequena* (it was small), *tinha um quintal* (it had a yard), *eu tinha dez anos* (I was ten).

grammars.title: Choosing between the two past tenses
body: The question isn't "when", but **"what job does this sentence do in the story"**. Background uses the *imperfeito*; events use the first past tense.
after: **The fourth row shows both in one sentence**, and that's the most typical pattern: *Chovia quando eu saí* = "It was raining when I left". The rain is the background (imperfeito), leaving is the event (first past). English marks this with "was …-ing"; Portuguese marks it with the verb form.
**Quick test:** if the sentence can be translated with "used to", "was …-ing" or "back then it was", use the **imperfeito**. If it fits "then", "next" or "one day", use the **first past tense**.
⚠️ Don't confuse this with "already" and "not yet". Both tenses are finished past; the only difference is how the story is told.

grammars.title: Old habits
body: Two extra formulas that sharpen the meaning "used to".

head: Português
Literally
English
rows: I used to get up early.
I used to go every Sunday.
I always used to study at night.

after: *Quando eu era criança* is the standard opener for a childhood story, and it will start many warm conversations in Brazil — Brazilians love telling stories about their childhood.
**Costumava** is used when you want to stress that the habit **has stopped**. Without it, the *imperfeito* alone is enough.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Note *a criança* — a **feminine** word, even when the child is a boy. The same goes for *a pessoa* (person) and *a vítima* (victim). Grammatical gender doesn't always follow reality.
This word deserves a page of its own, because it turns up in song titles, shop names, tattoos and everyday conversation.

head: Português
Literally
English
rows: I am with longing of you
I am with longing of home
to catch up after missing someone

blocks.text: Notice that the pattern uses *estar com* from unit 3 — once again, a feeling that Portuguese "has" rather than "feels". And *matar a saudade* is a lovely expression: easing the longing by seeing someone again, or by eating a food you haven't had for ages.

When you say goodbye to a Brazilian friend, the right line is *Vou ficar com saudade* — "I'm going to miss you". It will be warmly received, because it shows you've grasped something deeper than grammar.

exercises.prompt: Choose the right form: imperfeito or the first past tense.
items: Quando eu ____ criança, eu brincava na rua. (ser)
When I was a kid, I lived in Jakarta.
The house was small but it had a huge backyard.
I played with the neighbors every day.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: Eu morava em Jacarta. — Ela comia muito. — Nós brincávamos na rua. — Eles abriam a loja às oito. — Eu era criança. — Eu tinha dez anos.
